transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Well, I came in today because... I just feel like I can't settle inside my own skin anymore. It's just constant. Even when I'm completely worn out and I know I should be sitting still, I get this feeling like I have to jump up and do the next thing. I just can't seem to rest.
How long has this feeling of not being able to settle been going on—did it start suddenly at some point, or has it been present for as long as you can remember?
Well, it hasn't been my whole life, not like this anyway. It really started causing real trouble since my husband died. That was about... a year and ten months ago.
Since your husband passed away, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or empty most of the day, nearly every day?

No, not really. I mean, I miss him terribly, obviously, and there was grief... but I don't feel sad or empty all day long. It's not a depressed feeling. I just... I just have this constant need to be doing something, and I can't turn it off.

Along with this restlessness, have you noticed yourself worrying excessively about different things—like your health, finances, or family—more days than not, and finding it hard to control that worry?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have normal concerns like anybody else, but I'm not sitting around agonizing over my health or money or anything. My mind isn't really racing with worries like that. It's just... that physical feeling of needing to be up and doing something, not anxiety about things going wrong.
Have you noticed that you need much less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy, or that your mood has felt unusually high, elated, or irritable during this time?

No, my sleep is about the same as it's always been. I definitely don't feel like I'm full of energy or elated or anything like that. I'm just... restless. My mood is fine, I just can't seem to sit still.
Have you been using any substances lately—like caffeine, energy drinks, stimulant medications, cocaine, or other drugs—more than usual since your husband passed away?

No, nothing like that. I mean, I have my regular cup of coffee in the morning like I always do, but that's it. I haven't been drinking more of it, and I definitely haven't started taking any kind of... drugs or stimulants or anything. So it's not from anything I'm taking.
Since your husband's death, have you found yourself feeling hopeless, tearful, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, even if you wouldn't call it sadness?

No, I wouldn't say that. I miss him, of course, but I haven't felt hopeless or... or lost interest in my day-to-day life. I still like doing the things I usually do. I'm not crying all the time or feeling down in that way. It's really just the restlessness that's bothering me.
Do you find yourself frequently longing for your husband or preoccupied with thoughts of him and the circumstances of his death, in a way that feels intense or hard to move past?

No, not really. I mean, I think about him, obviously, because we were married a long time. But I'm not... consumed by it or anything. I'm not dwelling on how he died or constantly longing for him in a way that stops me from going about my day. It's just a normal amount of missing him, I think. It doesn't feel intense or like I'm stuck on it.

She explicitly denies pervasive depressed mood, anhedonia, hopelessness, or excessive/uncontrollable worry, ruling out major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. She denies increased stimulant or substance use, ruling out substance-induced etiology. She also denies intense preoccupation with the deceased, yearning, or being unable to accept the loss, arguing against prolonged grief disorder. The symptom picture—restlessness/behavioral disturbance emerging in response to an identifiable stressor without meeting criteria for another specific disorder—is best captured by Adjustment Disorder, unspecified (F43.20).
